Why does mint feel cold?
Why does mint feel cold?
The mint isn't cooling
your mouth down.
Nerves in your mouth
carry a tiny cold
sensor:
a gate that opens when
the temperature drops.
Menthol,
the molecule in mint,
latches onto that same gate.
Now it opens at warmer
temperatures,
even in a warm mouth.
The nerve fires,
and your brain gets one
message: cold.
That's why a sip
of water after a mint
can feel icy.
The sensor is already primed.
Chili plays the same
trick on your
burning-heat sensor.
Mint isn't cold.
It just rings the cold alarm.
